content: Bronchiolitis is a prevalent respiratory condition affecting infants, particularly during their first year of life. In this condition, the sputum of affected infants contains an increased amount of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), which contributes to the formation of mucus plugs and obstruction of the airways. Recombinant human deoxyribonuclease (rhDNase) is an enzyme capable of breaking down extracellular DNA, and it has been hypothesized that its use could help clear mucus and alleviate airway obstruction in these patients. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of nebulised rhDNase on the severity and duration of viral bronchiolitis in children under 24 months of age who were hospitalised. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, covering studies up to August 2012. The inclusion criteria focused on randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of nebulised rhDNase, either alone or in combination with other therapies, in hospitalised children under 24 months with acute bronchiolitis. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies, extracted data, and performed analyses using Review Manager 5.1. The treatment effects were expressed as mean differences (MD) or standardised mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Unpublished data were also obtained from trial authors. Three RCTs involving a total of 333 participants were included in the analysis. Two of these trials were multicentre studies that exclusively enrolled participants who tested positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), while the third trial included patients clinically diagnosed with bronchiolitis in an Italian hospital. All studies administered 2.5 mL (1 mg/mL) of nebulised rhDNase, either once or twice daily, and compared it to a placebo. Adjunctive therapies included nebulised salbutamol, steroids, supplemental oxygen, intravenous fluids or tube feeding, nasal washing, nasal decongestants, and antibiotics. The results showed that nebulised rhDNase did not provide any clinically meaningful benefits. Meta-analysis indicated that the control group had a shorter duration of hospital stay (MD 0.50 days; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.90, P = 0.01) and better clinical score improvement (SMD -0.24; 95% CI -0.50 to 0.01, P = 0.06). The largest trial found no significant differences in the use of supplemental oxygen or the need for intensive care unit (ICU) admission. In one RCT, four out of 11 patients in the treatment group developed atelectasis, and two of these patients showed notable clinical improvement after receiving nebulised rhDNase. However, there was no significant difference in the occurrence of adverse events between the treatment and control groups. Reported adverse events included temporary desaturation, temporary coughing, increased coughing, facial rash, hoarseness, dyspnoea, and bad taste, affecting a total of 11 patients across both groups. The authors concluded that the evidence from the three included studies does not support the use of nebulised rhDNase in children under 24 months of age hospitalised with acute bronchiolitis. The treatment did not reduce the length of hospitalisation or improve clinical outcomes. While nebulised rhDNase might have a potential role in cases of severe bronchiolitis complicated by atelectasis, further clinical studies are necessary to confirm its efficacy in such scenarios.
